knowledge_points.label: Verifiable rewards: optimize exactly what you want, so overoptimization stops binding
knowledge_points.statement: RLHF optimizes a learned proxy of preference and cannot be scaled out cleanly because the policy overoptimizes the proxy; RLVR works in domains (math, code) where the reward is the thing itself, so optimizing harder keeps buying real performance as long as the checker cannot be gamed, which is what carried models from ~GPT-3.5-level RLHF to o1/R1-level reasoning.

anchors.quote: With RLHF: we can't cleanly scale out due to overoptimization ... Can we work in domains where RL excels? Where we optimize exactly what we want
Pre-training + RLHF gets you to ~ GPT3.5… Today we'll get all the way to o1/r1
Overoptimization is a problem.. RL in narrow domains is one solution
I ended last lecture with this a little bit of a downer note ... you can't keep putting compute into the same reward model, eventually you're going to overfit your reward model

in AlphaGo, we are optimizing exactly what we want. You get the win-loss conditions of the game of Go. You don't have any sloppiness to that definition. And so you can just put in as much compute as you want.

In some sense, these are search problems. Whereas the top one is much more of a learning problem. Not quite a precise distinction ... formal mathematics or even natural language mathematics, that have this flavor of being more verifiable
the algorithms aren't going to be that different fundamentally, but where we will end up will actually be surprisingly different

the core takeaways of this lecture is it's really all about the reward for RL. RLHF and RLVR arguably they're very similar problems. ... we want more unhackable rewards so that we can actually put in much more compute

'Narrow domains' (p61) is the professor's own hedge: the recipe is presented as working where a checker exists, not as a general replacement for RLHF (p35 and p50 keep RLHF for non-verifiable tasks). Spoken evidence (1:11-1:49), a correction to 'assumed from the previous deck, not re-argued': the overoptimization argument is re-stated aloud in one breath: RLHF is 'fundamentally very annotation bottleneck', and 'you can't keep putting compute into the same reward model, eventually you're going to overfit your reward model', however well you regularize. Spoken evidence (2:06-2:57): the contrast that defines 'optimize exactly what we want' is AlphaGo, whose win-loss condition has no 'sloppiness', so 'you can just put in as much compute as you want'; he calls these search problems against RLHF's learning problem, 'not quite a precise distinction', and names formal and natural-language mathematics as the verifiable candidates. Spoken evidence (3:01): 'the algorithms aren't going to be that different fundamentally', which is the first misconception's why_wrong said aloud; the recap repeats it: 'RLHF and RLVR arguably they're very similar problems', the difference being 'more unhackable rewards' (1:09:16-1:09:39). The statement's 'optimizing harder keeps buying real performance' holds only while the checker is unhackable; see verifiable-reward-hacking. Statement not changed (no written claim is corrected; p3 and p61 stand).

external_prerequisites.note: Lecture 15 p62-p63 introduced reward overoptimization; this KP only asserts that a verifiable checker removes the proxy.

misconceptions.belief: RLVR is a new algorithm; the gain over RLHF comes from a better optimizer.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The optimizer family is the same (PPO/GRPO policy gradients, p18). What changes is the reward: a checker instead of a learned preference model, so there is no proxy to Goodhart and training can run longer.

misconceptions.belief: Because verifiable rewards are exact, reasoning RL replaces RLHF.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Every case study (R1 p35, Qwen 3 p50) still runs SFT/RLHF after reasoning RL for non-verifiable tasks; verifiable rewards only cover domains with a checker.

predict.q: You keep training an RLHF policy against a fixed reward model for 10x longer. Per slide 3, which quantity keeps rising and which one does not?
predict.answer: The reward-model score keeps rising; true human preference does not (overoptimization of the proxy).
predict.why: The reward model is a learned proxy; the policy finds outputs the proxy likes that humans do not. Slide 3's motivation for RLVR is exactly that this stops you from 'cleanly scaling out'.
predict.targets_misconception: RLVR is a new algorithm; the gain over RLHF comes from a better optimizer.

transfer.q: Task A: 'write a poem a reviewer will enjoy'. Task B: 'write a function that passes these hidden unit tests'. For which task does slide 3's argument say you can keep scaling RL compute without the reward decoupling from what you want, and what property of the reward makes the difference?
transfer.answer: Task B: the unit tests are the objective itself (verifiable), so optimizing them harder is optimizing what you want; Task A's reward is a learned proxy that can be overoptimized.
transfer.why: Verifiability means the reward is a checker, not a model of a judge; there is no gap between proxy and target for the policy to exploit.

check.q: A lab keeps its RL optimizer unchanged but swaps its learned reward model for a unit-test checker on coding tasks, and RL now keeps improving real performance as compute grows. Per slide 3, what made the difference?
choices: the checker gives denser rewards than the model did
the optimizer got better at following the reward
the reward now measures exactly what they want
check.answer: the reward now measures exactly what they want
check.why: p3: with RLHF you cannot cleanly scale out because the policy overoptimizes the learned proxy; in domains where you optimize exactly what you want, harder optimization keeps buying real performance. The optimizer is unchanged, and a pass/fail checker is if anything sparser than a reward model.
check.varies: the optimizer is held fixed and only the reward source changes, instead of comparing two tasks
check.invariant: RL scales when the reward is the objective itself rather than a learned proxy
check.targets_misconception: RLVR is a new algorithm; the gain over RLHF comes from a better optimizer.
distractor_from: 'the optimizer got better at following the reward' <- misconception: 'RLVR is a new algorithm; the gain over RLHF comes from a better optimizer.'
'the checker gives denser rewards than the model did' <- plausible: attributes the gain to reward density instead of reward validity

retrieval.q: In the professor's phrasing, what is special about the domains where 'RL excels'?
retrieval.answer: We optimize exactly what we want: the reward is the real objective (a checker), not a proxy.

knowledge_points.label: REINFORCE: the gradient of expected reward is E[R(z) grad log p(z)], and it is high-variance
knowledge_points.statement: The gradient of the expected reward under the policy equals the expectation of the reward times the score grad_theta log p_theta(z), so it can be estimated from samples without differentiating the reward; the professor's three-attempt story is that this estimator's variance is too high, TRPO fixes it by linearizing around the current policy, and PPO by clipping ratios at eps.

anchors.quote: Attempt 1: Policy gradients (variances are too high)
Attempt 2: TRPO (Linearize the problem around the current policy) ... Attempt 3: PPO (Clip the ratios at some eps)
A brief (and high level) intro to the various ideas in PPO..

The most important thing to identity, let's say to remember in RL for language modeling is policy gradients. And in particular this reinforce gradient trick. ... we are going to do so by taking essentially weighted SFT updates. The weights might be positive or negative.
this equation is important because it will reappear throughout this lecture. This is in some sense the core from which everything else is derived.

we want to take more than one step at a time. A policy gradient requires us to sample from our policy every time we want to take a gradient step. Can we reuse our rollouts? Well, you can do TRPO. You can do PPO
And I've already talked about TRPO. I won't really get too much into this.
I don't want to do reinforce-- vanilla reinforce because the variance of that is going to be really, really high.

misconceptions.belief: Policy gradients need the reward to be differentiable in the model's parameters.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The identity moves the gradient onto log p_theta(z); the reward R(z) is only a scalar weight on the score, so a non-differentiable checker (correct / incorrect) works.

misconceptions.belief: PPO and TRPO change the objective; they optimize something other than expected reward.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Per p5 they are variance-and-stability fixes to the same objective: TRPO linearizes around the current policy, PPO clips the ratio; at ratio = 1 both reduce to the plain policy gradient.

predict.q: Your reward is a unit-test checker returning 0 or 1, not differentiable in the model weights. Can the slide-5 policy-gradient estimator still be computed from samples?
choices: No, the reward must be differentiable
Yes, the reward only multiplies grad log p(z)
Only if a value network approximates the reward
predict.answer: Yes, the reward only multiplies grad log p(z)
predict.why: grad E[R] = E[R(z) grad log p(z)]: differentiation lands on the policy's log-probability, and R(z) enters as a scalar weight on each sampled sequence.
predict.targets_misconception: Policy gradients need the reward to be differentiable in the model's parameters.

transfer.q: Two sampled sequences get rewards +1 and 0 under the raw REINFORCE estimator. Which one contributes a nonzero gradient term, and in which direction does that term move the probability of the sampled sequence?
transfer.answer: Only the +1 sequence contributes (0 times the score is zero); its term increases log p of that sequence. The 0-reward sequence is ignored, which is one reason a baseline is added later.
transfer.why: Each term is R(z) grad log p(z); a zero reward contributes nothing, so without a baseline the estimator never pushes probability away from failures.

check.q: A checker returns +1 for a correct answer and -1 for a wrong one (instead of 1 and 0). With the raw REINFORCE estimator (reward times grad log p(z), no baseline) on a batch of 8 samples of which 3 are correct, how many of the 8 samples contribute a nonzero gradient term?
check.why: Each sample's term is R(z) grad log p(z). With rewards of +1 or -1, no term is multiplied by zero: the 3 correct samples push their log-probability up and the 5 wrong ones push theirs down. With 1/0 rewards only the 3 correct samples would contribute.
check.varies: the reward coding changes from 1/0 to +1/-1
check.invariant: the score-function estimator weights grad log p(z) by the reward; a zero reward contributes nothing

retrieval.q: What is the professor's one-phrase diagnosis of 'Attempt 1: policy gradients'?
retrieval.answer: Variances are too high.

retrieval.q: What does TRPO do to the problem and what does PPO do to the ratios?

presentations.notice: In the raw REINFORCE row a response with reward 0 gets no bar at all (its term is 0 times the score), so failures are never pushed down; with the ±1 coding preset every bar is nonzero and the wrong ones point down.

steps.why: Write the expectation as a sum over sequences. R does not depend on θ, so the gradient lands only on the probability.
This is the log-derivative identity. Multiplying by p turns the sum back into an expectation under the policy, so it can be estimated from samples.
Monte Carlo over rollouts. R is never differentiated: it is a scalar weight on an SFT-style log-likelihood gradient, positive or negative (4:04-4:28).

steps.do: Attempt 1 fails on variance. One scalar R multiplies the score of the whole sampled sequence, so each term swings with which sequence happened to be drawn.
steps.why: The estimator is unbiased but noisy, and every step needs fresh samples. Baselines lower the noise (baseline-validity-std-division). TRPO and PPO let one rollout be reused (4:38-4:54).

presentations.notice: listen for: policy gradient as 'weighted SFT updates' whose weights can be negative, and TRPO/PPO introduced as ways to reuse rollouts

knowledge_points.label: PPO: clip the probability ratio at 1 ± eps so a batch cannot move the policy far
knowledge_points.statement: PPO replaces the on-policy score with the importance ratio r = pi_new(z)/pi_old(z) weighted by the advantage, and takes min(r·A, clip(r, 1−eps, 1+eps)·A), so once the ratio leaves the band in the direction the advantage favours the gradient is zero and the update stops; AlpacaFarm uses Cliprange=0.2.

anchors.quote: The objective is basically all there is to it at a conceptual level
AlpacaFarm code – loss computation. Pretty standard stuff. ... Cliprange=0.2
PPO (Clip the ratios at some eps)
PPO, in case you're not familiar, is a real workhorse of RL.
So at a conceptual level, PPO is actually very simple.

You sample some trajectories. I compute something called an advantage using any method of advantage estimation. I clip the advantage in this slightly strange but OK way. And then I update the policy under this clipped advantage.
if you see a blog post that says the 37 implementation details of PPO, you know that this is an algorithm that is very sensitive to your implementation decisions.
The outer loop is fine. ... the actual inner compute loss part follows almost exactly the PPO update. ... We're computing things like the advantages and we're computing the clipping ratios.
implementations for RL algorithms can be somewhat tricky and somewhat sensitive because of all the moving pieces in PPO, and because of the high variance in the gradient estimates.

external_prerequisites.note: FeynRL's min(ratio*adv, clamp(ratio, 1-clip_low, 1+clip_high)*adv) is the same objective in code, with asymmetric clip bounds.

misconceptions.belief: Clipping caps the loss value, so a token whose ratio is outside [1−eps, 1+eps] still gets a (smaller) gradient.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The clipped term is a constant in theta, so when the min() selects it the gradient for that token is exactly zero: PPO stops moving that token rather than moving it less.

misconceptions.belief: The clip is symmetric: any ratio outside the band is ignored.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The min() keeps the unclipped term whenever it is lower. With A < 0 and r > 1+eps, r·A is more negative than the clipped term, so the token is still pushed down; only movement further in the advantage's favoured direction is stopped.

predict.q: eps = 0.2, advantage A = +1, and after a few inner steps a token's ratio is 1.5. What is the gradient of the PPO-clip objective with respect to that token's log-probability?
choices: Proportional to 1.5
Proportional to 1.2
Zero
predict.why: min(1.5·1, clip(1.5, 0.8, 1.2)·1) = min(1.5, 1.2) = 1.2, the clipped constant; its derivative in theta is 0. The ratio has already left the band in the favoured direction.
predict.targets_misconception: Clipping caps the loss value, so a token whose ratio is outside [1−eps, 1+eps] still gets a (smaller) gradient.

transfer.q: Same eps = 0.2 and ratio 1.5, but now the advantage is A = −1. Which term does the min() select, and does this token still receive a gradient?
transfer.answer: min(1.5·(−1), 1.2·(−1)) = min(−1.5, −1.2) = −1.5, the unclipped term; the token still receives a full gradient pushing its probability down.
transfer.why: Clipping is one-sided per sign of A: it only prevents moving further in the direction the advantage rewards. A ratio of 1.5 with negative advantage means the policy moved the wrong way, and PPO keeps correcting it.

check.q: PPO-clip with eps = 0.2: a token has advantage A = -1, and after a few inner steps its ratio pi_new/pi_old has fallen to 0.7. What gradient does this token receive from min(r·A, clip(r, 1-eps, 1+eps)·A)?
choices: a reduced one: clipping only caps the size of the loss
a full one: the unclipped term is the one the min() selects
none: the clipped term is selected, so the gradient is zero
check.answer: none: the clipped term is selected, so the gradient is zero
check.why: min(0.7 x (-1), 0.8 x (-1)) = min(-0.7, -0.8) = -0.8, the clipped term, which is constant in the parameters. The ratio has already moved past the band in the direction the negative advantage favours, so the update stops.
check.varies: negative advantage with the ratio below the band, instead of a ratio above the band
check.invariant: the min() selects the clipped term exactly when the ratio has left the band in the direction the advantage favours; then the gradient is zero
check.targets_misconception: Clipping caps the loss value, so a token whose ratio is outside [1−eps, 1+eps] still gets a (smaller) gradient.
distractor_from: 'a full one: the unclipped term is the one the min() selects' <- misconception: 'The clip is symmetric: any ratio outside the band is ignored.'
'a reduced one: clipping only caps the size of the loss' <- misconception: 'Clipping caps the loss value, so a token whose ratio is outside [1−eps, 1+eps] still gets a (smaller) gradient.'

retrieval.q: What quantity does PPO clip, and around which value?
retrieval.answer: The probability ratio pi_new/pi_old, clipped to [1−eps, 1+eps] around 1.

retrieval.q: What Cliprange value does the AlpacaFarm PPO implementation use?
For a positive-advantage token, what happens to the gradient once its ratio exceeds 1+eps?

knowledge_points.label: Language-model RL is a bandit: one terminal reward, so GAE with gamma = lambda = 1 is just reward-to-go minus value
knowledge_points.statement: In the language setting the actions are tokens and the single dense reward arrives at the end of the full sequence, so the episode is effectively a one-step bandit; with gamma = lambda = 1 the generalized advantage estimate collapses to the sequence reward-to-go minus the value baseline, and training curves look well-behaved.

anchors.quote: Actions operate over tokens, big dense reward at the very end operating on full sequence
Funny detail – this is a bandit problem and gamma=lambda=1 works – this is the reward-to-go vs the value
This is a bandit setting, you expect reasonable training curves

Notice how the green box appears twice. And importantly, some parts of my objective, the KL term, actually operates token by token. So it's not actually just a bandit problem. It's like a whole multi-step RL problem.

generalized advantage estimator that's basically looking at this gamma discounted reward ... people often just use gamma equals lambda equals 1, which is just a degenerate setting that turns this back into a bandit problem ... you've thrown away a lot of the structure that you get from PPO
if you run this algorithm after a bunch of engineering, you will get what you expect.
If we're in the bandit world, it's just the prompt. So you can have a prompt-dependent baseline that you can subtract.

misconceptions.belief: Discounting (gamma < 1) is needed for LM RL because sequences are long.
misconceptions.why_wrong: There is one reward at the end and no reason to prefer earlier tokens, so the professor notes gamma = lambda = 1 works: the advantage is the terminal reward minus the value estimate.

predict.q: With gamma = lambda = 1 and a single reward R at the last token, what does the GAE advantage for a token at position t reduce to?
predict.answer: R (the reward-to-go, plus any per-token KL shaping rewards after t) minus the value estimate V(s_t).
predict.why: gamma = lambda = 1 makes GAE the undiscounted Monte Carlo return minus the baseline; with only a terminal reward the return from every position is the same R.
predict.targets_misconception: Discounting (gamma < 1) is needed for LM RL because sequences are long.

transfer.q: An engineer sets gamma = 0.9 for a 500-token math solution with a terminal correctness reward. Roughly what happens to the credit the first token receives for a correct answer, and why does the slide's bandit view say this is a mistake?
transfer.answer: It is multiplied by about 0.9^500, essentially zero, so early tokens get no signal from correctness. In the bandit view the whole sequence is one action with one reward, so there is nothing to discount.
transfer.why: Discounting encodes a preference for sooner rewards across many decisions; here there is one decision (the sequence) and one reward, so gamma < 1 only destroys signal.

check.q: An engineer uses gamma = 0.99 (lambda = 1) for 300-token responses with a single terminal reward of 1 and no other rewards. By what factor is that reward discounted in the first token's return? Give a decimal.
check.why: The reward arrives 299 steps after the first token, so its weight is 0.99^299 = e^(299 ln 0.99) ≈ e^-3.0 ≈ 0.0495 (0.99^300 ≈ 0.049 is also accepted). Even a mild discount strips 95% of the credit; in the bandit view the sequence is one action, so gamma = 1.
check.varies: a mild discount (0.99) over 300 tokens instead of 0.9 over 500
check.invariant: discounting a single terminal reward shrinks early-token credit geometrically; the bandit view sets gamma = 1
check.targets_misconception: Discounting (gamma < 1) is needed for LM RL because sequences are long.

knowledge_points.label: Reward shaping: per-token KL penalty to the reference, full task reward on the last token
knowledge_points.statement: AlpacaFarm-style PPO adds a per-token penalty of log pi(token)/pi_ref(token) to the reward stream and places the full task reward on the last token; in practice the KL term is clipped for sequences where the new policy's log-probability is below the reference's, which keeps the KL estimate from diverging if the model blows up.

anchors.quote: High level – add per-token KL penalty, last-token full reward

misconceptions.belief: The task reward is spread over every token so that each token is rewarded for its contribution.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Per p14 only the last token carries the full task reward; intermediate tokens receive only the KL shaping term. Credit assignment within the sequence is the value model's job (and GRPO drops it entirely).

misconceptions.belief: The 'negative KL rewards' curve on slide 16 going down means training is failing.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The KL penalty is negative by construction and grows in magnitude as the policy drifts from the reference; a smooth decrease while total reward rises is the expected bandit-setting behaviour, not divergence.

transfer.q: During training the policy's log-probability on a sequence falls far below the reference's. Which direction of the per-token log-ratio does AlpacaFarm clip, and what failure does the professor say this prevents?
transfer.answer: It clips the KL term for sequences where new-policy logp < reference logp; this stops the KL estimate from diverging when the model 'blows up'.
transfer.why: A collapsed policy puts tiny probability on the reference's tokens, so log pi/pi_ref goes to minus infinity; clipping bounds the shaping term so one bad batch does not dominate the reward.

check.varies: the opposite direction of drift from the clipped case

transfer.q: You have a dataset of math problems with a correctness checker. Name the two properties of this data/training setup that slide 17 says make DPO a poor fit, and say which one 'iterating' would fix.
transfer.answer: The data are not pairwise (there is a scalar correct/incorrect reward per sample, not Bradley-Terry comparisons) and DPO is offline. Iterating DPO (re-sampling from the current policy) fixes the offline problem, not the pairwise one.

knowledge_points.label: GRPO: drop the value model, advantage = z-score of the reward within the prompt's group
knowledge_points.statement: GRPO keeps PPO's clipped-ratio loss and KL term but removes the value function: it samples a group of responses per prompt, computes each response's reward, and sets its advantage to (r − group mean)/(group std + a small stability term such as 1e-4); in the fully online case (rollout then immediate update) this is just policy gradient with group-normalized rewards.

anchors.quote: Start with PPO (many parts are similar) ... Remove the value function / advantage computation ... Calculate the advantage as "z-score within group"
In the online case (rollout+immediate update), this is just policy gradient with group normalized rewards
Compute reward for each rollout ... Mean/Var normalization per group ... Compute KL term ... Gradient updates on the loss
Basically just the 'vanilla' GRPO setup. ... Main difference here is just the 1e-4 stability factor in the std calculation

It changes arguably the most complicated and annoying part of PPO, which is the value function. So the value function is the thing that you subtract as a baseline to reduce variance of your gradient updates. The value function is a whole neural network. It destabilizes training.

let's say your rollout with a score of 5. You would now sample 10 other rollouts and you would say, how good was I compared to my 10 other rollouts. If I'm doing better than my mean, then I have a high advantage.

They're going to do exactly the PPO update, where they have this min clipped advantage, plus a KL term to keep yourself close to the reference. And then KL is computed in a particular way. That detail is not particularly important.

In the online case, the clipping just disappears because the ratio between pi theta old and pi theta is 1, this clipping operator never does anything and you just get min a of i, a of i. So this is just advantage minus a KL penalty.

I'm going to roll out k times, I'm going to compare my observed rollout to those k references, z-score it and then just take a reinforced gradient against those weights ... in order to do this using autodiff, you will have to do a stop grad somewhere

they add a little tiny weeny negative 4 to the standard deviation calculation to prevent it from blowing up when you only have a single sample, or if your samples happen to have the exact same rewards
this emphasizes to you how straightforward GRPO is, and why almost all open source work has been built on this algorithm.

misconceptions.belief: A correct answer always gets a positive advantage in GRPO.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The advantage is relative to the group: if every sample in the group is correct, every reward equals the mean and every advantage is 0 (no gradient from that prompt).

misconceptions.belief: GRPO replaces PPO's loss, not just its advantage.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p18: 'Start with PPO (many parts are similar)'; the ratio, clip and KL stay. Only the value-model advantage is replaced by the group z-score.

predict.q: A prompt's group of 4 samples all pass the checker (rewards 1, 1, 1, 1). What are the four GRPO advantages, and how much does this prompt contribute to the gradient?
predict.answer: All four advantages are 0 (each reward equals the group mean; the std term only keeps the division finite), so the prompt contributes no policy gradient.
predict.why: Group normalization measures 'better than my siblings'; a uniformly solved (or uniformly failed) prompt has no contrast to learn from. This is why difficulty filtering (p41, p51) matters.
predict.targets_misconception: A correct answer always gets a positive advantage in GRPO.

transfer.q: A group of 4 rewards is 1, 0, 0, 1. Using the population standard deviation (divide by 4) and ignoring the small stability term, compute the four GRPO advantages. Then: for rewards 1, 0, 0, 0, which has the larger magnitude, the correct sample's advantage or an incorrect one's?
transfer.answer: Mean 0.5, std 0.5: advantages +1, −1, −1, +1. For 1, 0, 0, 0: mean 0.25, std ≈ 0.433, so the correct sample gets ≈ +1.73 and each incorrect one ≈ −0.58; the lone correct sample has the larger magnitude.
transfer.why: z = (r − mean)/std. The rarer outcome sits further from the mean, so a single success in a mostly-failing group is pushed up hard while each failure is pushed down gently; the advantages always sum to 0.

check.q: A GRPO group of 5 samples gets rewards 1, 0, 0, 0, 0. Using the population standard deviation (divide by 5) and ignoring the small stability term, what is the advantage of the one correct sample?
check.why: Mean = 0.2; population variance = (0.8^2 + 4 x 0.2^2)/5 = 0.16, so std = 0.4. Advantage = (1 - 0.2)/0.4 = 2.0 (each wrong sample gets -0.5).
check.varies: group size 5 and a different reward pattern
check.invariant: GRPO advantage = (r - group mean) / group std

knowledge_points.label: Baselines: subtracting a state-dependent term is unbiased; dividing by the group std is not
knowledge_points.statement: Any term that depends only on the state (prompt) can be subtracted from the reward without biasing the policy gradient, so the group mean is a valid baseline; dividing by the group standard deviation is not a baseline and breaks unbiasedness, and Dr. GRPO's fix removes the std division (and the per-response length normalizer), landing close to REINFORCE with a leave-one-out baseline.

anchors.quote: The key difference in GRPO vs PPO: the advantage ... Baselining: We can subtract any state-dependent term from our rewards
The division by the stdev term is not a valid baseline that preserves unbiasedness.
Also note the modification on the length-normalizer term on the left.. ... Liu et al 2025. (this gets pretty close to reinforce w/ leave-one-out)

there's this algorithm called reinforce with baseline. ... I can subtract any-- what they call state-dependent baseline ... If we're in the bandit world, it's just the prompt. ... And anything that does just this is a valid form of a policy gradient.
depending on your choice of b, you will either have lower or higher variance in doing this gradient descent process.
We are not just subtracting a constant value, we are also dividing by the standard deviation. And so that is a problem.

it's in some ways a problem. In other ways, it's not. If you really want a conceptually clear algorithm that really does what's written on the tin, it actually descends the reward. GRPO does not do that.

if you try to derive GRPO from first principles, following the policy gradient and baseline theorems, you'll end up with something different. You won't have a length normalizer and you won't have the standard deviation normalization.
GRPO is not the first principles derivation of this idea. It is actually doing something slightly different with both pros and cons.

misconceptions.belief: Any per-prompt normalization of the reward (subtract mean, divide by std) is just a baseline and leaves the gradient unbiased.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Subtraction of a state-dependent term is unbiased because E[b(s) grad log pi(a|s)] = 0. Division rescales the whole gradient of each prompt by 1/std(s), which reweights prompts by how uncertain they are; it is a multiplicative change, not an additive baseline.

misconceptions.belief: A valid baseline must be learned (a value network).
misconceptions.why_wrong: Any state-dependent quantity works, including the empirical mean of sibling rewards in the group; Dr. GRPO and RLOO use exactly such sample-based baselines with no learned critic.

predict.q: Which of these changes to the per-sample weight on grad log p(z) keeps the policy-gradient estimator unbiased, per slides 22-23?
choices: Subtracting the group mean reward
Dividing by the group std
Both
Neither
predict.why: A subtracted state-dependent term has zero expected contribution; division by the std multiplies each prompt's gradient by a prompt-dependent factor and so changes the expectation.
predict.targets_misconception: Any per-prompt normalization of the reward (subtract mean, divide by std) is just a baseline and leaves the gradient unbiased.

transfer.q: Prompt A's group has rewards 1, 0, 0, 0 (std ≈ 0.43); prompt B's group has rewards 1, 1, 0, 0 (std 0.5). Compared with the unbiased mean-subtracted gradient, by what factor does GRPO's std division scale each prompt's contribution, and which prompt is upweighted?
transfer.answer: Each prompt's contribution is multiplied by 1/std: about 2.3x for A and 2x for B, so A (the harder, lower-variance prompt) is upweighted relative to B.
transfer.why: Dividing by a per-prompt constant rescales the prompt's whole gradient. Prompts whose rewards are nearly all the same (very easy or very hard) have small std and get the largest multiplier, which is p24's 'upweights too easy or hard questions'.

check.q: A GRPO group of 8 samples has rewards 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0. Relative to the unbiased mean-subtracted weights, by what factor does dividing by the group's population standard deviation (ignoring the stability term) scale this prompt's contribution to the gradient?
check.why: Population std = sqrt(p(1 - p)) with p = 1/8: sqrt(7/64) ≈ 0.331, so every weight is multiplied by 1/0.331 ≈ 3.02. Subtracting the mean is a valid state-dependent baseline; this extra prompt-dependent rescaling is not, so it biases the gradient toward near-uniform groups (p23).
check.varies: a larger group with one success instead of comparing two 4-sample prompts
check.invariant: the std division rescales each prompt's contribution by 1/std, which is not a baseline
check.targets_misconception: Any per-prompt normalization of the reward (subtract mean, divide by std) is just a baseline and leaves the gradient unbiased.

retrieval.answer: It must depend only on the state (the prompt), not on the sampled action/response.

knowledge_points.label: GRPO's two biases: std upweights too-easy/too-hard prompts, length normalization favours long wrong answers
knowledge_points.statement: GRPO's std division upweights prompts whose rewards are nearly uniform (too easy or too hard), and its per-response length normalizer divides each response's token gradients by its own length, so a wrong (negative-advantage) response is penalized less per token when it is long and a right response is rewarded less per token when it is long; Dr. GRPO removes both terms so length stops being favoured by the objective.

anchors.quote: Length biases of GRPO ... What do these terms do? Stdev – upweights too easy or hard questions. ... Length normalization: ... What does the fix do?
Also note the modification on the length-normalizer term on the left..
From some follow-up analyses in Dr. GRPO.. ... Length due to biased objective?
there's another thing that GRPO does ... GRPO does this almost per token. So they'll divide by the total length of the sequence as a normalization factor.

I know that I'm going to get a math proof wrong. I'm going to incur my negative reward of let's say, negative 1. I'm just going to generate an infinitely long string. If I do that, I'll get to divide by infinity, and I'll get to totally get rid of my negative penalty.
if you divide by the output, you encourage the model to blab on once it realizes that it cannot actually solve the problem.

If you fix that, you'll find that often what people have observed in GRPO COT, like chain of thought, thinking length growing and growing and growing, that actually turns out to just cap off at a constant rather than just continually and forever grow.

this can be thought of as emphasizing problems where the standard deviation is small. And when is my standard deviation small for a binary reward problem? Well, that's when the problems are too easy or too hard.

the standard deviation term is upweighting the two sides, both easy and hard questions. That seems like clearly a thing that maybe we don't want because we want our models to potentially learn on things that are within its solvability range.

provenance.filtering_note: The direction of the length bias (long wrong answers penalized less per token, long right answers rewarded less per token) is written on p24 only inside the image of the objective and the Dr. GRPO annotations; the text layer has just the headings. Dr. GRPO's plots (p30: response length vs steps for GRPO vs Dr. GRPO, and the length of incorrect responses) carry no numbers in the text layer. The fix is 'divide by a constant instead of the response length', which the slide shows but does not say aloud. Spoken evidence (23:46-24:29): the direction of the length bias, image-only on p24, is said aloud with an extreme case: a model sure to fail could 'generate an infinitely long string' and 'divide by infinity', so length normalization makes it 'blab on once it realizes that it cannot actually solve the problem'. The Dr. GRPO result is read aloud: with the fix, length growth 'turns out to just cap off at a constant rather than just continually and forever grow' (24:33-24:49). The fix is described aloud only as dropping the length normalizer (22:55); 'divide by a constant' is still not said, as above. Spoken evidence (25:03-25:56): the std term emphasizes 'problems where the standard deviation is small', which for binary rewards means 'too easy or too hard', and that is undesirable because models should learn on problems 'within its solvability range'. Author note: he says an always-solved question is divided by 'basically 0' (25:22); for an exactly uniform group the numerator is 0 too, so the advantage is 0 (the 1e-4 keeps it finite), and the upweighting bites on nearly uniform groups such as 1 success in 8. Spoken slip (23:55-24:06), self-corrected and garbled: 'it's going to encourage the model to generate long outputs because-- or sorry when you're wrong it will encourage you to generate wrong outputs'. He means long outputs when wrong, as the next sentences show. Not imported. Slide image audit (p23): the Dr. GRPO objective on the image drops the 1/|o_i| factor, leaving a plain token sum; 'divide by a constant' is equivalent up to the learning-rate scale.

misconceptions.belief: Normalizing each response's loss by its length is neutral: it just averages per token.
misconceptions.why_wrong: With a sequence-level advantage, dividing by length makes a long negative-advantage response lose less total probability mass than a short one, and a long positive one gain less. The gradient then favours long failures and short successes; that is a length bias, not an average.

misconceptions.belief: The std division helps because it focuses learning on the hardest prompts.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It upweights any prompt with low reward variance, which includes the easiest (nearly all correct) ones as much as the hardest; p24: 'upweights too easy or hard questions'.

predict.q: Two wrong responses to the same prompt get the same negative advantage; one is 100 tokens, the other 1,000. Under GRPO's per-response length normalization, which response's tokens are pushed down less per token?
choices: The 100-token response
The 1,000-token response
Equal per-token push
predict.why: Each response's token gradients are divided by its own length, so the same advantage is spread over 10x more tokens in the long answer: being wrong at length is cheaper, which pushes the policy toward long wrong answers.
predict.targets_misconception: Normalizing each response's loss by its length is neutral: it just averages per token.

transfer.q: An engineer removes the std division but keeps per-response length normalization, then observes average response length still climbing on prompts the model mostly fails. Which of GRPO's two biases is still active, and what replacement for the per-response normalizer does Dr. GRPO make?
transfer.answer: The length bias from the per-response normalizer is still active (long wrong answers are penalized less). Dr. GRPO divides by a constant (a fixed maximum length) instead of each response's own length, so the per-token penalty no longer shrinks with length.
transfer.why: The two biases are independent: std affects prompt weighting, length normalization affects within-response weighting. Only replacing the per-response denominator with a constant removes the second.

check.q: Under GRPO's per-response length normalization, two correct responses to one prompt both have advantage +1; one is 300 tokens and the other 1,200. How many times larger is the per-token gradient weight on the 300-token response?
check.why: Each response's token gradients are divided by its own length, so the per-token weight is A/|o|: 1/300 versus 1/1200, a factor of 4. A long right answer is rewarded less per token, mirroring how a long wrong answer is penalized less; Dr. GRPO's constant normalizer makes the factor 1.
check.varies: correct responses (positive advantage) and a numeric ratio, instead of a diagnosis with the std term removed
check.invariant: per-response length normalization makes the per-token weight inversely proportional to the response's length
check.targets_misconception: Normalizing each response's loss by its length is neutral: it just averages per token.

retrieval.q: Why does GRPO's division by the group std give extra weight to prompts that are too easy or too hard?
retrieval.answer: Their sampled rewards are nearly all the same, so the group std is small and dividing by it gives a large multiplier.

retrieval.q: Which two terms of the GRPO objective does Dr. GRPO change?
retrieval.answer: It removes the division by the group std and replaces the per-response length normalizer with a constant.

presentations.notice: Under GRPO, responses with the same verdict sit on one Â/length curve, so a response with 4× (or 10×) the tokens gets 1/4 (1/10) of the per-token weight; under Dr. GRPO their open dots share one flat line whatever their length.

steps.why: GRPO averages each response's token terms over that response's own length before averaging over the group (22:29-22:48).

steps.do: The predict's case: two wrong responses with Â = −1, of 100 and 1,000 tokens. Per-token weight Â/|o|: −1/100 = −0.01 against −1/1,000 = −0.001.
steps.why: The same advantage is spread over 10× more tokens, so each token of the long answer is pushed down 10× less.

steps.do: A wrong answer gets cheaper per token the longer it is. A right answer gets less reward per token the longer it is.
steps.why: A model that cannot solve the problem lowers its penalty by rambling, the 'divide by infinity' argument (24:06-24:29). For right answers the same division favours short ones.

steps.do: Dr. GRPO divides by a constant instead of |o_i| (and drops the std, which upweights too-easy and too-hard prompts).
steps.why: With a constant denominator the per-token weight is Â/const whatever the length, so the objective no longer favours length. Thinking length then 'caps off at a constant' (24:33-24:49).

knowledge_points.label: R1-Zero: GRPO on the V3 base model with only accuracy and format rewards, no PRM, no MCTS
knowledge_points.statement: DeepSeek-R1-Zero applies GRPO directly to the DeepSeek-V3 base model with two rewards, an accuracy reward (is the answer correct?) and a format reward (use the thinking tags), with no process supervision and no search; it matches or beats OpenAI o1-0912 on math (AIME cons@64 86.7 vs 83.3, MATH-500 95.9 vs 94.8) while trailing on code, and the paper's unsuccessful-attempts section (PRMs, MCTS) ended speculation that those were necessary.

anchors.quote: Rewards ... Accuracy rewards (is it correct?) ... Format rewards (use thinking tags) ... Data (not public) ... Base model: Deepseek-V3 ... Results: a bit worse than Openai O1
Open RL recipe (that is also pretty simple) ... Ended speculations on the necessity of MCTS/PRMs
They build on the results of GRPO from DeepSeekMath.. ... But they do not use process supervision in R1
There is a whole unsuccessful attempts section ... PRMs ... (PRM800k, DeepseekMath) ... MCTS
I think it was really the first thing to have matched OpenAI O1's behavior. ... And they also provided RL recipe that anyone could do.

they abandon process supervision, which was the thing that worked really well in DeepSeekMath, and they go only with outcome supervision. And just to be clear, outcome supervision is when you have reward only for whether the final answer is correct or incorrect.

process supervision is when you have a grading rubric, let's say, to check the validity of intermediate steps in a proof. A lot of people thought process supervision was important. Turned out it wasn't critical for a lot of things.

the rewards for their GRPO algorithm is accuracy ... and format rewards. And this one is important because the format rewards basically allow them to strip out the chain of thought later. They want the model to properly use thinking tags to enclose their COT.
And where do you end up? Well, you end up something that is only a little bit worse than OpenAI O1. ... It's a very simple base model plus GRPO.

we tried to get process reward models to work. They just didn't do very much for us. It turns out that outcome reward models are great and they're good enough. And you can scale the data for those a lot better. I think a big debate for PRMs was, where are you going to get these step-by-step rubrics.
a lot of people speculated about what was going on inside OpenAI's O1. ... Are they doing tree search like AlphaGo? They to tried a lot of MCTS and they describe we couldn't get it to work very well.

provenance.filtering_note: The R1-Zero results table (p28) and the R1 benchmark table (p36, 'It's pretty good (but you knew that)') are images; no AIME/MATH numbers are in the text layer. The exact format reward (think/answer tags) and how the accuracy checker handles math vs code are not stated. The slide says the training data is not public. p21's DeepSeekMath figure, 'Outperforms RFT (reinforcing correct answers), with some gains from process supervision', is the deck's only evidence for process supervision helping, and p27/p38 record that R1 dropped it anyway. Spoken evidence (28:15-28:36): outcome and process supervision are defined aloud (reward 'only for whether the final answer is correct' vs 'a grading rubric ... to check the validity of intermediate steps'). Spoken evidence (29:11-29:21), partly answering 'the exact format reward ... not stated': the format reward's purpose is said, the thinking tags 'allow them to strip out the chain of thought later'; the tag strings are still not given. This supports the format-reward misconception's why_wrong. Spoken evidence (37:05-37:38): why PRMs lost: 'outcome reward models are great and they're good enough', 'you can scale the data for those a lot better', while step-by-step rubrics are 'very hard to scale'. MCTS 'couldn't get it to work very well' (37:57). R1-Zero is 'only a little bit worse than OpenAI O1' and praised as 'a very simple base model plus GRPO' with no production confounds (29:35-29:57). Spoken imprecision (28:02): process supervision 'worked really well in DeepSeekMath'; p21 says only 'some gains from process supervision'. Caption error: 'the base model ... is also [? MIT ?] trained' (28:50) is presumably 'mid-trained'. Not imported. Slide image audit (p28): the earlier 'a bit below o1' is not what the table shows; R1-Zero beats o1-0912 on AIME 2024 cons@64 (86.7 vs 83.3) and MATH-500 (95.9 vs 94.8) and trails on code (LiveCodeBench, Codeforces). Statement corrected.

misconceptions.belief: R1-Zero needed a process reward model to score each reasoning step.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p27-p28: only an outcome accuracy reward and a format reward; the R1 paper lists PRMs (and MCTS) under unsuccessful attempts (p38).

misconceptions.belief: The format reward is there to improve answer accuracy.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It rewards using the thinking tags so the output is parseable and the reasoning is separable from the answer; accuracy is a separate reward.

predict.q: Which pair of rewards did R1-Zero train with, per slide 28?
choices: Accuracy + per-step process reward
Accuracy + format (thinking tags)
Format + MCTS search value
Accuracy + learned preference model
predict.why: R1-Zero used exactly two outcome-level rewards; process rewards and MCTS are in the paper's unsuccessful-attempts section.
predict.targets_misconception: R1-Zero needed a process reward model to score each reasoning step.

transfer.q: A response contains a correct final answer but no thinking tags. Under R1-Zero's two rewards, which reward component is nonzero and which is zero, and what will the policy be pushed toward over training?
transfer.answer: Accuracy reward is earned, format reward is not; the policy is pushed to keep answering correctly and also to wrap its reasoning in the thinking tags, since tagged correct answers score higher within the group.
transfer.why: Rewards are summed, and the group z-score ranks siblings; untagged correct answers sit below tagged correct ones in the same group.

check.q: Under R1-Zero's two rewards, a response wraps a long chain of reasoning in the thinking tags but gives a wrong final answer. What does it earn?
choices: neither, without a process reward for each step
both, since tagged reasoning counts toward accuracy
the format reward only, not the accuracy reward
the accuracy reward only, not the format reward
check.answer: the format reward only, not the accuracy reward
check.why: p28: the accuracy reward checks whether the answer is correct and the format reward checks the thinking tags; they are independent, and R1-Zero uses no process supervision (p27).
check.varies: the format is right and the answer wrong (inverse of the correct-but-untagged case)
check.invariant: R1-Zero scores outcome accuracy and tag format separately, with no step-level reward
check.targets_misconception: The format reward is there to improve answer accuracy.
distractor_from: 'both, since tagged reasoning counts toward accuracy' <- misconception: 'The format reward is there to improve answer accuracy.'
'neither, without a process reward for each step' <- misconception: 'R1-Zero needed a process reward model to score each reasoning step.'
'the accuracy reward only, not the format reward' <- plausible: swaps which reward checks the tags

retrieval.q: What base model did R1-Zero start from, and what was done to it before RL?
retrieval.answer: DeepSeek-V3 base; nothing (no SFT), GRPO was applied directly.

retrieval.q: Which two techniques does the R1 paper's unsuccessful-attempts section cover?
retrieval.answer: Process reward models (PRMs) and Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS).

retrieval.q: How did R1-Zero compare with OpenAI o1, in the professor's words?
retrieval.answer: A bit worse than o1.

knowledge_points.label: Longer CoTs and the 'aha moment': what R1-Zero showed and what Dr. GRPO says about it
knowledge_points.statement: R1-Zero's training curves show response length growing over training and the paper reports an 'aha moment' of self-reflection; Dr. GRPO's follow-up argues the length growth is partly an artifact of GRPO's biased length normalization and that base models already exhibit 'aha' phrasing before any RL, so neither phenomenon is clean evidence that RL created new reasoning behaviour.

anchors.quote: Interesting phenomena (?) ... Longer CoTs during training ... 'aha' moment?
But maybe a bit overstated ... From some follow-up analyses in Dr. GRPO.. ... Length due to biased objective? ... Base model already has 'aha'

anchors.ref: dr-grpo:§2 base models already exhibit aha; §3 length

anchors.quote: as we go longer and longer and longer during training, the model is able to think for longer and longer and longer. ... the aha moment

It is unclear to me whether either of these phenomena are really particularly impressive in many ways. We now know that longer CoTs is arguably a natural side effect of the length normalization of the GRPO algorithm. And the aha moment others have showed is actually appears in even the base model.
And so clearly, it can't just be a result of the RL algorithm. Lots of people say aha, I can use this as part of solving the math problem. The model has learned it during pre-training.
I think the phenomena that was highlighted is not particularly salient or exciting, but I do think R1 was a really important milestone in that it highlighted just how simple RLVR could be.

provenance.filtering_note: Both slides are images: the R1 length-vs-step plot and the 'aha moment' transcript (p29), and Dr. GRPO's length plots and base-model 'aha' keyword counts (p30). No lengths, step counts or keyword frequencies are in the text layer. The professor's own position is hedged ('maybe a bit overstated'); the slide does not settle how much of the length growth survives the Dr. GRPO fix, only that some of it is attributable to the objective. Spoken evidence (30:34-31:18), a correction to 'The professor's own position is hedged': aloud he is firmer than p30's 'maybe a bit overstated': 'We now know that longer CoTs is arguably a natural side effect of the length normalization', and the base-model 'aha' means 'clearly, it can't just be a result of the RL algorithm'. He gives the reason the slide lacks: people write 'aha' when solving math, 'the model has learned it during pre-training', and RL extracts it. The statement's 'partly an artifact' is kept: he says 'arguably', and the Dr. GRPO plot discussed at 38:41-39:52 (see incorrect-responses-drive-length-growth) shows growth that caps off rather than vanishes. Slide image audit (p30): the image shows one example base-model response containing 'Aha!', not keyword counts; 'keyword counts' above is wrong.

prerequisites.note: The Dr. GRPO critique on p30 reuses the p24 length-bias mechanism.

misconceptions.belief: Response length growing during RL proves the model learned to think longer because it helps accuracy.
misconceptions.why_wrong: GRPO's per-response length normalizer makes long wrong answers cheaper, so length can grow for reasons unrelated to accuracy; Dr. GRPO shows part of the growth disappears once the objective is unbiased.

misconceptions.belief: The 'aha moment' (self-reflection phrases appearing) is a behaviour RL created from nothing.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p30: the base model already produces 'aha'-style phrases before RL; RL may amplify them but did not invent them.

predict.q: You switch an R1-Zero-style run from GRPO to Dr. GRPO (unbiased objective) and nothing else. Per slide 30, what should happen to the growth of response length on prompts the model gets wrong (up / down / same)?
predict.answer: down: the growth should slow or shrink, because part of it was caused by the biased length normalizer rewarding long wrong answers.
predict.why: Removing the per-response length division removes the incentive for wrong answers to be long; whatever growth remains is attributable to the task, not the objective.
predict.targets_misconception: Response length growing during RL proves the model learned to think longer because it helps accuracy.

transfer.q: A blog claims 'the base model never says wait, let me reconsider; RL taught it self-reflection.' Which single measurement that Dr. GRPO ran (and slide 30 cites) would test this claim, and what did it find?
transfer.answer: Count 'aha'/self-reflection phrases in the base model's outputs before any RL; Dr. GRPO found the base model already produces them.
transfer.why: The claim is about a before/after difference, so the control is the base model's own sampling; p30: 'Base model already has aha'.

check.q: An RL run uses GRPO with per-response length normalization, and average response length doubles over training. Which conclusion does slide 30's follow-up evidence support?
choices: part of the growth may come from the biased objective
the model learned that longer thinking raises accuracy
RL created reasoning the base model never showed
check.answer: part of the growth may come from the biased objective
check.why: p30, citing Dr. GRPO: length growth may be due to GRPO's biased length normalization, and the base model already shows 'aha' phrasing. Neither phenomenon is clean evidence that RL created new reasoning.
check.varies: the evidence is length growth rather than 'aha' phrases
check.invariant: R1-style length growth and 'aha' moments are confounded by the objective and by base-model behaviour
check.targets_misconception: Response length growing during RL proves the model learned to think longer because it helps accuracy.
distractor_from: 'the model learned that longer thinking raises accuracy' <- misconception: 'Response length growing during RL proves the model learned to think longer because it helps accuracy.'
'RL created reasoning the base model never showed' <- misconception: 'The 'aha moment' (self-reflection phrases appearing) is a behaviour RL created from nothing.'

retrieval.q: What two phenomena of R1-Zero training does the lecture list, each with a question mark?
retrieval.answer: Longer chains of thought during training, and an 'aha' moment.

retrieval.q: What two counter-explanations does Dr. GRPO offer?
retrieval.answer: Length growth is partly due to the biased objective; the base model already shows 'aha' behaviour.

prompts.self_explain: Why is a plot of mean response length against training steps insufficient to separate 'learned to reason longer' from 'learned that long wrong answers are cheap'?

The widget draws only the objective's push, which is why the same rising length curve cannot by itself say whether reasoning got longer for a reason.

knowledge_points.label: The R1 recipe: V3 → reasoning SFT (cold start) → GRPO with language-consistency reward → SFT/RLHF → distil
knowledge_points.statement: R1 differs from R1-Zero by starting from a reasoning SFT (cold start on long-CoT data; even ~1k samples bootstraps reasoning), adding a language-consistency reward during GRPO, then running the usual SFT (2 epochs on 600k reasoning samples judged by V3 plus 200k non-reasoning samples) and RLHF for non-verifiable tasks, after which 800k R1 traces are distilled into Qwen 2.5 models; per slide 54, the general RLHF stage costs a little math/STEM (the professor ties the drop to Qwen3's thinking-mode fusion, and the Qwen3 report shows small math/coding losses across both fusion and general RL).

anchors.quote: Key differences: ... SFT initialization ... Language consistency reward for CoT ... Non-verifiable rewards (in stage 2) ... Deepseek-V3 ... Reasoning SFT ... RL (GRPO) ... SFT/RLHF
Even a small number of samples is effective for bootstrapping reasoning from LMs ... 1k Math and science questions + Long CoTs from Gemini / r1
Minor difference: additional language consistency loss ... RL naturally leads to mixed languages?
SFT step, 2 epochs. ... Reasoning data – non-verifiable tasks ('write a proof of X'), use V3 as a judge (600k) ... Non-reasoning data – V3 SFT dataset (200k) ... Still uses GRPO (for RLHF)
Have R1 generate CoT traces (800k!) ... Teach Qwen 2.5 via distillation
RLHF comes after reasoning RL (like r1), distillation after that.
Note that math/stem abilities go down (a bit) with general purpose RLHF

how do we compose all of the pieces to actually get a system at the end? ... And then we're going to do RLHF at the end, because that's in some sense, the most user-facing object. We want to make sure that the formatting and all of this is nice.

they added a language consistency reward for the chain of thought ... without a consistency reward would language switch in COT, and they thought this was very uninterpretable and slightly disturbing. ... they do this just for interpretability reasons.
When they say something like, we construct and collect a small amount of long COT data, you might wonder-- I wonder if that was distilled from some other models.
We know that for a very good base model, just SFT on long COT can unlock a lot of O1 style capabilities. And that's a great starting point for RL.

one of the things that I think is still an open question is, do you really need RL for some of this. ... RL is a great source of supervision. ... once someone has generated these long CoTs, you could potentially also learn from imitation.
you can then take R1's CoTs and you could put it into Qwen 2.5, and if you did so, you could really significantly boost the performance of these models. ... this works even for Llama models as well

We do base model to basically SFT, then reasoning RL. And then they have this thinking mode fusion. ... And then they do RLHF and then they have a model that gets shipped. ... So they do distillation to get their smaller models.
There are some degradations that we see in math and coding because we fuse together non-thinking components, but the degradation is not so bad.
the reasoning problems all go in one bucket and they get executed at stage II. And then the non reasoning problems happen at the final RLHF phase.

provenance.filtering_note: The '1k samples' claim on p33 comes from a figure the slide does not attribute; it matches s1 (Muennighoff et al. 2025) by content (basis: inference). p32 notes the cold-start data origins are 'not quite clear' and the claimed benefit is interpretability. The distillation results table (p37) and the Qwen 3 stage-composition table (p54, where the math/STEM drop is read off) are images with no numbers in the text layer. Whether distillation into Qwen 2.5 beats running RL directly on the small model is in the R1 paper but not on the slides. Spoken evidence (32:06-32:23): why RLHF goes last: it is 'the most user-facing object', where formatting is fixed. Spoken evidence (32:27-32:51), answering p34's 'RL naturally leads to mixed languages?': yes, R1-Zero-style training 'would language switch in COT', and the consistency reward is added 'just for interpretability reasons'. Spoken evidence (33:24-33:50), on p32's 'origins on the data not quite clear': he reads 'collect a small amount of long COT data' as probably distilled from other models. Spoken evidence (34:13-34:56): RL as 'a great source of supervision' for problems with no long CoTs, which imitation can then copy; 'do you really need RL' is called an open question (this framing was considered as a spoken KP and rejected as hedged). Distillation also works into Llama models (36:36; R1 paper, not on p37). In Q&A, reasoning and non-reasoning data are split between the reasoning-RL stage and the final RLHF stage (1:15:05-1:15:30). Recorded disagreement (1:00:34): he attributes the p54 math/coding drop to fusing in non-thinking data ('because we fuse together non-thinking components'); p54 attributes it to general-purpose RLHF. The Qwen3 report (arXiv:2505.09388, author check) reports the drop after both Thinking Mode Fusion and General RL. He does not retract p54, so the statement and the transfer item keep the slide's wording. He adds that later Qwen 3.5 releases separated the thinking and non-thinking models again (1:00:43-1:01:05).

external_prerequisites.note: The 'usual post-training process' on p35 is lecture 15's SFT then RLHF.

misconceptions.why_wrong: p31 and p50: the order is reasoning SFT, reasoning RL (GRPO), then SFT/RLHF for general behaviour, then distillation. RLHF after reasoning RL costs a little math/STEM (p54).

misconceptions.belief: Distillation here means matching the teacher's logits.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p37: R1 generates 800k CoT traces and Qwen 2.5 is fine-tuned on them; it is SFT on teacher samples.

predict.why: p31's pipeline arrow (V3 → Reasoning SFT → RL (GRPO) → SFT/RLHF) and p50 ('RLHF comes after reasoning RL, distillation after that').

choices: Surprising: RLHF trains on general chat, so math should not move
Expected: general RLHF after reasoning RL costs a bit of math/STEM
Surprising: RLHF normally runs before reasoning RL, not after it
Expected: the distillation step always loses some accuracy
transfer.answer: Expected: general RLHF after reasoning RL costs a bit of math/STEM

'distillation always loses accuracy' <- related to misconception 'Distillation here means matching the teacher's logits.' (misplaces distillation in the pipeline and its role)
'math should not move' <- plausible: assumes stages trained on different data do not interact

knowledge_points.label: GRPO's length pressure is asymmetric: right answers hit a length floor, wrong ones grow without bound
knowledge_points.statement: Under GRPO's per-response length normalization the two length pressures do not cancel: correct responses are pushed shorter but cannot shrink below the minimum reasoning the problem needs, while incorrect responses are pushed longer with no upper bound, so the net length growth is driven by the incorrect responses and is largest where the model fails most; Dr. GRPO's split plot shows the growth sitting in the incorrect responses.

anchors.quote: So the question was like for positive cases what the length normalizer do. And of course, in those cases, the length normalizer encourages you to shorten the COT, which is good if you want to save on inference costs, bad if that degrades your accuracy.

for the negative ones, you get some really long responses and the positive cases, it can't shrink it that much because there's a lower bound to how small your COT can go to solve a particular problem.

in the R1 diagram, this is all aggregated. ... It's not just the positive ones. ... this is like the average output length and this is the incorrect output length. ... this is really being driven by the incorrect ones as we would expect from the explanation.
you encourage the model to blab on once it realizes that it cannot actually solve the problem.
especially on the incorrect cases, you really don't want to be generating longer and longer and longer outputs.
Length due to biased objective?

anchors.ref: dr-grpo:§3.1 length bias (output length of incorrect responses)

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only (a Q&A answer, 38:25-39:58). The slides give the two directions of the bias only inside the p24 image and show Dr. GRPO's plots (p30) with no text beyond 'Length due to biased objective?'. The asymmetry argument (a lower bound on how short a correct CoT can be, no upper bound on a wrong one) and the reading of the split plot ('really being driven by the incorrect ones') are said aloud; he also notes that R1's own length curve aggregates all responses, so it cannot show this. The failure-rate dependence (more growth where more responses are wrong) is the author's direct consequence of his argument, and the numbers in the prompts are the author's. He frames the result as holding 'at least in these sets of controlled comparisons'.

misconceptions.belief: The length normalizer's two pushes cancel: correct answers shrink about as much as incorrect ones grow, so mean length should stay roughly flat.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Correct answers cannot shrink below the reasoning the problem needs ('a lower bound to how small your COT can go'), while wrong answers can grow without limit, so the net effect is growth (38:55-39:09).

misconceptions.belief: Length growth under GRPO comes mostly from correct responses becoming more thorough.
misconceptions.why_wrong: In Dr. GRPO's split plot the growth is 'really being driven by the incorrect ones' (39:30-39:52); the normalizer pushes correct responses shorter, not longer.

choices: run A, where most responses are correct
run B, where most responses are wrong
the same in both runs, since the pushes cancel

transfer.q: Under GRPO's per-response normalization, a correct 200-token answer is already the shortest that solves its problem, and an incorrect answer to a harder problem is 2,000 tokens. Which of the two can still respond to the length pressure, in which direction, and what does this predict for the mean length of a batch that is half correct and half incorrect?
transfer.answer: Only the incorrect one: it is pushed longer and has no ceiling. The correct one is pushed shorter but is at its floor. The batch's mean length rises, carried by the incorrect half.
transfer.why: The pressure on correct answers saturates at the problem's minimum length; the pressure on wrong answers does not saturate, so the average drifts upward.

check.q: Over a stretch of GRPO training with per-response length normalization, 60% of responses are incorrect and each grows by 300 tokens, while the 40% correct responses each shrink by 50 tokens before reaching their floor. By how many tokens does the mean response length change? Give a signed number.
check.why: 0.6 x 300 = 180 tokens of growth from the incorrect responses against 0.4 x 50 = 20 tokens of shrinkage from the correct ones, a net +160. The shrinkage is capped by the floor; the growth is not, so the mean rises.
check.varies: a concrete mixture of correct and incorrect responses, instead of comparing two runs
check.invariant: correct responses can shrink only to a floor while incorrect ones grow without bound, so net length rises with the share of failures
check.targets_misconception: The length normalizer's two pushes cancel: correct answers shrink about as much as incorrect ones grow, so mean length should stay roughly flat.

retrieval.answer: There is a lower bound on how short a CoT can be and still solve the problem; wrong answers have no upper bound.
