knowledge_points.label: Kimi's DPO-style loss differentiates into a policy gradient with GRPO's group-mean baseline (no std, no length division)
knowledge_points.statement: Kimi k1.5 reaches its loss by a DPO-style route (solve the KL-regularized objective in closed form, then put a squared loss on the equality that holds at the optimum), yet the gradient of that surrogate is a policy gradient whose baseline is the mean reward of the k responses sampled for the same prompt, plus a regularizer term: GRPO's group-mean baseline, without GRPO's division by the group standard deviation or by each response's length. Two unrelated derivations landing on the same per-prompt mean baseline is the lecture's evidence that this baseline, not the PPO machinery, is the component that matters.

anchors.quote: the interesting thing about Kimi is that they have a DPO inspired argument, but they end up actually in a place that's very similar as GRPO. And I think the fact that they end up in similar places is suggestive of which of these components are potentially useful
And therefore, this is a big heuristic. If something's equal at the minimizer, why don't we just put a squared loss on that thing and minimize the squared loss?

you take a gradient of this L, you end up with something that looks surprisingly like GRPO with an added regularizer term. What you end up with is this thing that is a policy gradient with a baseline R bar. And that R bar is actually the mean of each condition, these x's.
this additional regularizer term, which is essentially the KL term that would appear in GRPO. So in some sense, we've reinvented the group mean normalized baseline through quite different means.
if you look at this objective, they don't normalize by sequence length
RL algorithm inspired by DPO-type derivation. ... Use squared loss as a surrogate ... Baselined policy gradient w/ regularization

anchors.ref: kimi:§2.3.2 policy optimization (r̄ = mean of the k sampled rewards)

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only for what the baseline is. Slide p42's text layer says 'Baselined policy gradient w/ regularization' and 'Use squared loss as a surrogate'; the objective, the closed-form step and the gradient are images. Aloud (43:53-46:25) he walks the derivation, calls the squared loss 'a big heuristic' that 'optimization people ... would be horrified at' but a 'totally reasonable intuition', identifies the baseline as 'the mean of each condition' (per prompt), and concludes 'we've reinvented the group mean normalized baseline through quite different means'; at 47:06 he adds that the objective does not normalize by sequence length. That the baseline is the plain mean, with no std division, is read from the Kimi paper's gradient (arXiv:2501.12599: r̄ = mean(r(x, y_1, y*), ..., r(x, y_k, y*)), author check); he says 'group mean normalized', which the prompts take as mean-subtracted. The paper's gradient also carries a common 1/k factor and a squared log-ratio regularizer with coefficient tau; the prompts ask for per-sample weights up to that common factor and ignore the regularizer. Including the sample's own reward in the mean scales every weight by (k - 1)/k relative to a leave-one-out baseline (the RLOO point of p23); the prompts do not depend on this. The inference 'this baseline is the component that matters' is his ('suggestive of which of these components are potentially useful', 44:03), hedged.

prerequisites.note: The comparison is with GRPO's mean subtraction (a valid baseline) and std division (not one).

misconceptions.belief: Kimi's update also z-scores rewards within the group, like GRPO.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Its gradient subtracts the per-prompt mean reward r̄ and nothing else: no division by the group std and no per-response length normalizer (47:06), so its weights are r - r̄.

misconceptions.belief: A DPO-style derivation produces a preference-style update, so Kimi's algorithm has nothing in common with GRPO.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The squared surrogate's gradient is a policy gradient with a per-prompt mean baseline plus a KL-like regularizer, which is GRPO's group-mean baseline reached 'through quite different means' (45:45-46:25).

predict.q: Kimi samples k = 4 responses to a prompt and the checker gives rewards 1, 0, 0, 0. Ignoring the regularizer term and the common 1/k factor, what weight multiplies grad log p of the correct response in the gradient of Kimi's surrogate loss?
predict.why: The baseline is the mean reward of the 4 samples, 0.25, so the correct response's weight is 1 - 0.25 = 0.75 (each wrong one gets -0.25). GRPO would also divide by the group std (about 0.433) and give about 1.73.
predict.targets_misconception: Kimi's update also z-scores rewards within the group, like GRPO.

transfer.q: A new paper derives an RL loss from a maximum-entropy argument that never mentions PPO, and its gradient turns out to be the sum over the k samples of (r_j - mean of the k rewards) times grad log p(y_j | x), plus a KL-like term. Using the lecture's reading of Kimi, what does this suggest about which ingredient matters, and how does this estimator treat a prompt whose rewards are 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0 compared with GRPO?
transfer.answer: It is a third derivation landing on the per-prompt mean baseline, which suggests the mean baseline is the useful ingredient rather than any one derivation. It does not divide by the std, so the 1-in-8 prompt keeps weights 0.875 and -0.125, whereas GRPO would multiply them by about 3.02 (1/std), upweighting this near-uniform prompt.
transfer.why: Mean subtraction is a state-dependent baseline (p22); the std division is the extra, biasing reweighting (p23-p24). Convergent derivations point at the shared part.
transfer.varies: a third, unrelated derivation and a near-uniform group, instead of Kimi's own loss
transfer.invariant: the per-prompt mean baseline is what different derivations share; the std division is GRPO's addition

check.q: A group of 5 responses gets rewards 1, 1, 0, 0, 0. GRPO's z-score (population std) gives each correct response about 1.22. Under Kimi's gradient (mean baseline only; ignore the regularizer and the common 1/k factor), what weight does each correct response get?
check.why: The group mean is 2/5 = 0.4, so each correct response's weight is 1 - 0.4 = 0.6 and each wrong one's is -0.4. GRPO divides these by the population std sqrt(0.24) ≈ 0.49, giving about 1.22 and -0.82; Kimi's gradient has no such division.
check.varies: a 5-sample group with two successes, with GRPO's value given for contrast
check.invariant: Kimi's per-sample weight is the reward minus the per-prompt mean, with no std division
check.targets_misconception: Kimi's update also z-scores rewards within the group, like GRPO.

retrieval.q: What baseline appears in the gradient of Kimi's squared-loss surrogate, per the professor?
retrieval.answer: r̄, the mean reward of the responses sampled for the same prompt (plus a KL-like regularizer term).

retrieval.q: Which two GRPO normalizations are absent from Kimi's objective?
retrieval.answer: The division by the group standard deviation and the per-response length normalization.

retrieval.q: What step in Kimi's derivation does the professor call 'a big heuristic'?
retrieval.answer: Putting a squared loss on an equality that holds only at the optimum and minimizing it as a surrogate.

prompts.self_explain: Why is it evidence about which ingredient matters when a DPO-style derivation and a PPO-style derivation both end at a per-prompt mean baseline?

presentations.notice: Kimi's gradient weight is the 'mean baseline' row, r minus the group's mean reward: the GRPO row without its 1/std factor, so on a near-uniform group the two rows differ by that whole factor.
listen for: the 'big heuristic' squared loss, and its gradient turning into 'a policy gradient with a baseline R bar' that is the per-prompt mean

knowledge_points.label: Kimi k1.5 length reward: lambda in [0.5, −0.5] by rank, correct answers pushed short, wrong ones below the centre
knowledge_points.statement: Kimi's DPO-derived squared-loss policy gradient does not have GRPO's length bias, but to compress CoTs further it adds a per-batch length reward: within a group each response gets lambda in [0.5, −0.5] with the longest sequences negative; correct answers receive lambda (so shorter is better), incorrect answers receive min(0, lambda) (so they are pushed shorter than the centre of the group's length range), and the term is switched on only later in training because of its effect on performance.

anchors.quote: The kimi objective doesn't have the same GRPO length bias problem. ... But they want to further compress the CoTs. ... For each batch, they have a length reward

The lambda is in [0.5, -0.5], with longer sequences in a group being negative ... Correct answers are incentivized to be short ... Incorrect answers are incentivized to be shorter than the center of the range of rollouts
(They also only enable this later on in traning, due to its effects on perf)
RL algorithm inspired by DPO-type derivation. ... Use squared loss as a surrogate ... Baselined policy gradient w/ regularization

if we're making long CoTs potentially, that's very wasteful. We don't really want long CoTs because CoTs cost inference. So not only do they not have a length problem, because if you look at this objective, they don't normalize by sequence length

when we think for very long, we have to essentially subsidize the user. If you're OpenAI and your users have the $200 Pro Plan, and your models are thinking for an hour at a time, that's not a very good place to be in.
you come up with a heuristic length reward and you just tack it on to the RL process. This reward is surprisingly complicated. ... Correct answers also should be short.

if you make the incorrect answers too short, they no longer have a way to recover. ... Imagine I'm bad at geometry. ... the penalty makes my geometry CoTs really short. ... I will never get a positive geometry reward ever again.
you don't force the incorrect answers to be super short. You incentivize them to be just a little bit shorter than the average, so that the incorrect stuff doesn't grow unboundedly.

as RL proceeds, you're able to think longer and performance goes up. ... You're not thinking for that much longer, but your performance continues to go up. So maybe this is a good example of this length control kicking in

provenance.filtering_note: The length-reward formula (p43) and the Kimi objective (p42, 'Nonparametric assumption + solve for r') are images; the exact lambda formula (0.5 − (len − min_len)/(max_len − min_len)) and the min(0, lambda) rule for incorrect answers are read from the image and from the paper, not from the text layer. The slide does not say what 'later' means in steps. Kimi's reference-based reward model and the DPO-derivation are mentioned only at the level of the quotes above. Spoken evidence (47:06-47:19): why Kimi has no GRPO length bias: 'they don't normalize by sequence length'. The motive for compressing anyway is inference cost: long thinking means you 'subsidize the user' (47:28-47:49). Spoken evidence (48:22-49:02), the reason for the min(0, lambda) rule that the slide states without argument, and the answer to this KP's self-explain: if incorrect answers are pushed all the way short, 'they no longer have a way to recover' (a model bad at geometry whose geometry CoTs shrink to nothing 'will never get a positive geometry reward ever again'), so wrong answers are only kept from growing 'unboundedly'. The p47 scaling plots are read as length control at work: on OmniMath performance rises without much longer thinking (54:19-54:51). 'Only later in training' is not said aloud. Spoken imprecision (48:53): 'a little bit shorter than the average'; p43 says 'shorter than the center of the range of rollouts' (the midpoint of min and max length, not the mean). Not imported.

prerequisites.note: The slide contrasts Kimi's situation with GRPO's length bias.

misconceptions.belief: A length penalty should push every response to be as short as possible.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Kimi's rule treats correct and incorrect responses differently: correct ones are rewarded for being short, incorrect ones are only penalized when longer than the group's centre (min(0, lambda)), so there is no reward for a short wrong answer.

misconceptions.belief: Kimi needs the length reward because its objective has GRPO's length bias.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p43 says the Kimi objective does not have that bias; the length reward is a deliberate extra compression target, enabled late to protect performance.

predict.q: In a Kimi group the longest response is wrong and the shortest response is wrong. Using lambda in [0.5, −0.5] by length rank and the slide's rule for incorrect answers, which of the two gets a nonzero length reward, and what sign?
predict.answer: Only the longest wrong response: lambda = −0.5 (negative). The shortest wrong response has lambda = +0.5 but incorrect answers get min(0, lambda) = 0.
predict.why: Incorrect answers are incentivized to be shorter than the centre of the range, not to be short per se; a positive lambda is never paid out for a wrong answer.
predict.targets_misconception: A length penalty should push every response to be as short as possible.

transfer.q: Two correct responses to the same prompt: one is the shortest in its group, one is the longest. What length rewards do they receive under the Kimi rule, and what does this do to the policy's preferred CoT length on prompts it already solves?
transfer.answer: Shortest correct: +0.5; longest correct: −0.5. On solved prompts the policy is pushed toward the shortest CoT that still gets the answer right.
transfer.why: Correct answers receive lambda directly, so among correct siblings rank by length is the entire signal; the task reward is already equal across them.

check.q: Under Kimi's per-group length reward (lambda from +0.5 for the shortest to -0.5 for the longest; correct answers get lambda, incorrect answers get min(0, lambda)), which incorrect responses are pushed to get shorter?
choices: none: only correct answers receive a length reward
all of them, toward the shortest length in their group
only those longer than the centre of the group's range
check.answer: only those longer than the centre of the group's range
check.why: p43: incorrect answers get min(0, lambda), which is negative only where lambda < 0, i.e. for responses longer than the centre of the range; shorter wrong answers get 0. Incorrect answers are incentivised to be shorter than the centre, not as short as possible.
check.varies: incorrect responses across the whole range instead of the two extreme correct ones
check.invariant: correct answers get lambda; incorrect answers get min(0, lambda)
check.targets_misconception: A length penalty should push every response to be as short as possible.
distractor_from: 'all of them, toward the shortest length in their group' <- misconception: 'A length penalty should push every response to be as short as possible.'
'none: only correct answers receive a length reward' <- plausible: forgets the min(0, lambda) term for incorrect answers

retrieval.answer: [0.5, −0.5]; longer sequences in a group are negative.

retrieval.q: What is the difference between how Kimi's length reward treats correct and incorrect answers?
retrieval.answer: Correct answers are incentivized to be short (receive lambda); incorrect answers are only pushed to be shorter than the centre of the group's length range (no positive reward).

retrieval.q: When during training does Kimi enable the length reward, and why?
retrieval.answer: Only later on, because of its effect on performance.

knowledge_points.label: Data for RLVR: keep prompts the model fails at best-of-n, drop guessable formats, go easy to hard
knowledge_points.statement: Kimi and Qwen 3 filter RL prompts for difficulty by sampling the current model n times (Kimi: drop problems the model can guess within 8 tries without CoT, since those are easy to hack; Qwen: remove problems solved without CoT, remove near-duplicates of validation data), exclude multiple-choice and true/false items because they produce false-positive rewards, and Kimi additionally orders training easy-to-hard and samples prompts proportional to (1 − success_rate) so solved problems are not repeated; Qwen 3 runs GRPO on only 3,995 such examples.

anchors.quote: Exclude multiple choice / true false (false positives) ... Select only examples that models fail on best-of-8
Assign difficulty labels to dataset, go from easy to hard ... Sample problems proportional to (1-success_rate) to avoid repeating solved ones
Filtering for difficulty (by best-of-n, like kimi) ... Remove things that the model gets right w/o CoT ... Remove things too similar to validation data ... RL with GRPO on only 3995 examples
For code – take problems with ground truth solutions, generate new test cases ... For math – 800k samples to train a CoT reward model for answer equivalence checks

anchors.ref: kimi:§2.2 prompt set curation; §2.3.5 sampling strategies

anchors.quote: for RL, there's an additional wrinkle of curriculum ... if your problems are too hard, you get no rewards. And if you get no rewards, you have no signal. And if you have no signal, you can't learn.
they exclude multiple choice because that's covered in lots of different domains. They want things that require long, deep thought. And their argument is maybe multiple choice doesn't have that.

you filter them based on a best of k filter. ... if they succeed on best of 8, if you sample eight times and the model can do it at least once, then that's not a great RL example ... you only look at examples that basically fail this test

And so this saves compute. ... You can also filter on both sides to get problems that are neither too hard nor too easy. I think the general consensus in the research community is that doing this medium range difficulty filtering is very good
they also look at the success rates of how often they're able to solve particular problems. And once the model masters a particular problem, it gets taken out of the problem set.

for code, they take ground truth solutions and they generate some new test cases. And for math, they actually have a reward model to check for answer equivalence checks. ... we ended up with a reward model, a reward model that checks the correctness of math answers.

answer equivalence checking is a very difficult problem. ... most RL projects have a very complicated answer checker, either a regex or a model ... It's a real rabbit hole getting the verified part of RLVR.

They do a lot of filtering for difficulty because we know that saves compute. ... they remove things that the model can get right without COT because we know that's not a thinking problem. ... they actually do their RL on very few examples, just 4,000 examples.

provenance.filtering_note: The slides do not say how many prompts Kimi kept after filtering, what n Qwen used for best-of-n, or how 'too similar to validation data' was measured. Kimi's SFT stage is described as 'little description, just described as prompt engineering (distillation?)' (p41). p44's math reward uses a trained CoT reward model for answer-equivalence checking, which is a learned verifier rather than a pure checker; the slide does not flag the tension with 'verifiable'. Spoken evidence (41:37-42:12): why difficulty matters in RL and not in SFT: 'if your problems are too hard, you get no rewards ... no signal ... you can't learn'. He adds what p41 omits: 'you can also filter on both sides' for medium difficulty, the 'general consensus' (43:26-43:44). Spoken evidence (49:55-51:10), a correction to 'the slide does not flag the tension with verifiable': he flags it at length: the lecture began with compiler-checkable math and 'ended up with a reward model ... that checks the correctness of math answers'; strict checkers fail on correct answers written differently (a missing or padded \boxed), so 'most RL projects have a very complicated answer checker, either a regex or a model', 'a real rabbit hole'. Qwen 3's prompts not solvable 'without COT' are removed because that is 'not a thinking problem' (57:22). Recorded disagreement (42:26-42:36): aloud, multiple choice is excluded because Kimi wants 'things that require long, deep thought'; p41 says '(false positives)', and the Kimi paper (arXiv:2501.12599, author check) gives false-positive verification as the reason, matching the slide. Author check against the Kimi paper, flagged for review: the best-of-8 test is a no-CoT guessing test: 'we prompt a model to guess potential answers without any CoT reasoning steps. If the model predicts the correct answer within N attempts, the prompt is considered too easy-to-hack and removed' (N = 8); difficulty itself is estimated from the pass rate of ten sampled answers. p41 and the professor (42:43-43:10) drop 'without CoT', and his reading (keep only problems the model cannot solve once in 8 samples) sits against his own 'too hard ... no signal' and 'filter on both sides'. The statement follows p41 ('keep only problems failed on best-of-8') and is not changed; with the paper's reading it matches Qwen's 'remove things the model gets right w/o CoT'. Spoken imprecisions: 'just 4,000 examples' for p51's 3,995 (57:41); a mastered problem 'gets taken out of the problem set' (49:25) for p44's sampling proportional to (1 - success_rate); 'already at the edge of the model's capabilities' (42:55) for problems the model already solves.

prerequisites.note: Uniformly solved or uniformly failed groups give zero advantage, which is why difficulty filtering matters for GRPO.

misconceptions.belief: More RL prompts are always better; data volume drives RLVR gains as in pretraining.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Qwen 3 used only 3,995 prompts after filtering (p51); prompts the model already solves (or always fails) give no group contrast and waste rollouts.

misconceptions.belief: Multiple-choice questions are ideal for RLVR because they are trivially verifiable.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p41: they are excluded because guessing yields false-positive rewards; the checker is exact but the signal is noisy.

knowledge_points.label: Why RL is hard to make efficient: on-policy rollouts are slow inference, framework switching, uneven long-CoT batches
knowledge_points.statement: On-policy RL spends most of its wall-clock in rollouts, which is autoregressive inference and slow; switching between training and rollout usually means two different frameworks and a weight transfer; and long chains of thought make batch lengths very uneven, so the systems side (utilization, overlap) matters as much as the algorithm.

anchors.quote: Systems and utilization aspects of RL are very important. ... Why is RL hard to make efficient?
On policy = rollouts, which means (slow) inference ... Switching from training to rollouts often means different frameworks ... Long CoTs can make batches very uneven.
Kimi's RL setup in detail
RL infra is really quite hard. Training is hard and inference is hard. And RL puts the two together.

imagine you've got your rollouts, but you've got one really hard math problem, let's say one of them is like the Riemann hypothesis. ... everyone else is waiting on this one rollout to complete in order to move on to the next phase.

some CoTs can get really long. Do you need to truncate them, do you somehow set them into a different machine, who knows? ... Either some of your machines are pure rollout machines, and some of them are training machines, or you're switching out frameworks all the time. Both of them are very costly.

on policy stuff is mathematically and training dynamics wise very nice. ... if only I could reuse my rollouts, then I can overlap my inference and computation ... And that will lead to off-policy problems which then lead to destabilizing your training

That's the blue boxes over here and an inference part, which is the green part on the right. And you're going to have to move weights from the training part to the inference part. ... maybe they even share the same machines because as inference is running, the training one might be idle.

provenance.filtering_note: Kimi's infrastructure diagram (p46: rollout workers, trainer, replay buffer, weight sync) is image-only; no GPU counts, rollout-to-train ratios or throughput numbers are in the text layer. The slide does not quantify the rollout share of time nor discuss partial rollouts, async/overlap training or staleness budgets; FeynRL's sync vs overlap modes (feynrl:sync-epoch-loop, feynrl:staleness-budget-max-lag) are the concrete version. p55-p60 (Qwen3-Coder-Next: 600 billion tokens of repository-level mid-training data, 800k automatically constructed SWE-bench-style environments, expert models distilled into one) extend the systems story to agentic RL and are not made into KPs. Spoken evidence (51:42-52:17): the uneven-batch point is given a picture: one rollout on 'the Riemann hypothesis' with a gigantic CoT while 'everyone else is waiting on this one rollout'. Spoken evidence (52:24-53:31), a correction to 'does not ... discuss partial rollouts, async/overlap training or staleness budgets': he names truncation or moving long rollouts to another machine as options, dedicated rollout vs training machines against switching frameworks ('Both of them are very costly'), and the central trade-off: on-policy GRPO 'behaves very nicely', but reusing rollouts to overlap inference and training 'will lead to off-policy problems which then lead to destabilizing your training'. This is the answer to this KP's self-explain. Staleness budgets are not named. The p46 diagram is read aloud: training (blue) and inference (green) parts, weights moved between them, and possibly shared machines because 'the training one might be idle' (53:37-54:11). Still no numbers. Slide image audit (p46): the image shows Megatron and vLLM sidecars in one pod with a checkpoint engine and offload/onload, and no replay buffer; 'replay buffer' above is wrong.

prerequisites.note: A group of G samples per prompt multiplies the rollout cost by G.

What overlapping rollout and training buys and what it costs in off-policy drift.

misconceptions.belief: RL training cost is dominated by the gradient steps, as in pretraining.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p45: on-policy RL means generating fresh rollouts every step, and autoregressive generation of long CoTs is slow inference; the training GPUs idle while rollouts run unless the two are overlapped.

misconceptions.belief: Padding uneven sequences is a minor cost.
misconceptions.why_wrong: With long CoTs one response in a batch can be many times longer than the rest, so the whole batch waits on the longest generation; p45 lists this as a first-class inefficiency.

predict.q: In a synchronous loop where one rollout phase takes 4 time units and one training phase 3 (plus 0.5 for weight sync, during which no training happens), what fraction of the time are the training GPUs busy training?
predict.why: 3/(4+3+0.5) = 0.4; the rest of the time they wait for inference. This idle share is what the 'systems and utilization aspects' on p45 are about.
predict.targets_misconception: RL training cost is dominated by the gradient steps, as in pretraining.

transfer.q: You double the group size G per prompt and switch from short-answer prompts to long-CoT prompts whose lengths vary 10x within a batch. Name the two of slide 45's three inefficiencies that get worse, and the one that is unchanged.
transfer.answer: Worse: slow on-policy inference (twice as many rollouts, each longer) and uneven batches (10x length spread). Unchanged: the framework switch between training and rollout, which is a per-step fixed cost.
transfer.why: Rollout volume and length variance scale with G and CoT length; the training/inference framework boundary is independent of them.

check.q: A rollout batch of 8 sequences is generated together and finishes only when its longest sequence does: 7 sequences stop at 1,000 tokens and one runs to 8,000. What fraction of the batch's generation slots (8 sequences x 8,000 steps) hold real tokens? Give a decimal.
check.why: Real tokens: 7 x 1,000 + 8,000 = 15,000. Slots: 8 x 8,000 = 64,000. Fraction = 0.234, so about three quarters of the batch's decode slots are idle padding. This is slide 45's 'long CoTs can make batches very uneven'.
check.varies: a concrete uneven batch instead of naming which inefficiencies worsen
check.invariant: synchronous batched decoding runs to the longest sequence, so length spread wastes capacity
check.targets_misconception: Padding uneven sequences is a minor cost.

retrieval.q: Name two of the three reasons the lecture gives for RL being hard to make efficient.
retrieval.answer: Any two of: on-policy RL needs rollouts, which are slow inference; training and rollouts use different frameworks; long CoTs make batch lengths very uneven.

retrieval.q: Why does the rollout phase of an on-policy RL step take far more wall-clock than the policy update on the same tokens?
retrieval.answer: Rollouts are autoregressive inference, one token per step (slow); the update is a single parallel forward/backward over whole sequences.

knowledge_points.label: RL vs RFT / expert iteration: learning from negative gradients, not only from correct samples
knowledge_points.statement: Rejection-sampling fine-tuning (RFT) and expert iteration train only on positive (correct) samples; GRPO additionally pushes probability away from incorrect samples via negative advantages, and both DeepSeekMath (GRPO over RFT, with some further gain from process supervision) and Kimi's ablation against expert iteration report that the full RL signal wins.

anchors.quote: GRPO from the original paper ... Outperforms RFT (reinforcing correct answers), with some gains from process supervision
Ablation / comparison to expert iteration ... Could we avoid RL-style negative gradients and just learn from positives?

They show that GRPO, the yellow and the blue lines, does much better than RFT, like rejection fine tuning. You'll implement this as a baseline as well. That's just taking the correct answers that your model generates and training on them and throwing away everything else.
they seem to show process supervision, which is grading not just the final answer, but grading the intermediates give you some gains. I'll talk more about that later.

is this actual RL stuff much better than just training on correct answers. This is called expert iteration. It worked very well in a number of past papers. In cases where you're dealing with very unstable stuff, you may actually want to do expert iteration instead.

Kimi K1 has very large scale ablations showing that these kinds of RL methods work consistently better than expert iteration. So that's the orange beating the blue over here. So you can't really avoid RL if you want to squeeze out all of your performance.

provenance.filtering_note: Both comparisons are plots (p21 DeepSeekMath GSM8K/MATH curves; p48 Kimi expert-iteration ablation) and no accuracy numbers appear in the text layer; the size of the gap is image-only. The slide poses p48 as a question and lets the figure answer it; the professor does not discuss why negatives help (they also sharpen the distribution and remove probability mass from plausible-but-wrong modes) or the cases where positive-only training is competitive. p21's 'some gains from process supervision' sits in tension with R1 later dropping PRMs (p27, p38). Spoken evidence (19:24-19:38): RFT is defined aloud ('taking the correct answers that your model generates and training on them and throwing away everything else') and is an assignment baseline. Spoken evidence (54:51-55:29), a partial correction to 'or the cases where positive-only training is competitive': expert iteration 'worked very well in a number of past papers', and 'in cases where you're dealing with very unstable stuff, you may actually want to do expert iteration instead'; Kimi's ablation (orange over blue) shows RL 'consistently better', so 'you can't really avoid RL if you want to squeeze out all of your performance'. Why negatives help is still not said aloud. 'Kimi K1' (55:10) is k1.5.

prerequisites.note: Negative advantages are the baseline-shifted counterpart of the 0-reward terms that raw REINFORCE ignores.

misconceptions.belief: Filtering for correct samples and fine-tuning on them (RFT / expert iteration) is equivalent to RL with a correctness reward.
misconceptions.why_wrong: RFT only raises the probability of correct samples; GRPO's group z-score gives wrong samples negative advantages, so it also lowers their probability. p21 and p48 show the RL versions ahead.

predict.q: Which training signal does RFT (reinforcing correct answers) lack that GRPO has, per slides 21 and 48?
choices: A reward for correct answers
Negative gradients on incorrect answers
A format reward
A learned value model
predict.why: RFT keeps only correct samples and does SFT on them; GRPO assigns below-mean rewards negative advantages, pushing wrong samples down.
predict.targets_misconception: Filtering for correct samples and fine-tuning on them (RFT / expert iteration) is equivalent to RL with a correctness reward.

transfer.q: A group of 4 rewards is 1, 0, 0, 0. Under RFT, how many of the four samples enter the update and with what sign? Under GRPO (mean-subtracted), how many enter and with what signs?
transfer.answer: RFT: 1 sample, positive. GRPO: all 4; the correct one positive (+0.75 before std scaling) and the three wrong ones negative (−0.25 each).
transfer.why: RFT is SFT on the filtered positives; GRPO's advantages are reward minus group mean, so every sample carries a signed contribution that sums to zero.

check.q: A group of 5 samples gets rewards 1, 1, 1, 0, 0. Under GRPO with mean subtraction only (no std division), what advantage does each wrong sample get? Give the signed value.
check.why: Group mean = 3/5 = 0.6, so each wrong sample gets 0 - 0.6 = -0.6 and each correct one +0.4. Under RFT the two wrong samples would contribute nothing; GRPO pushes their probability down.
check.varies: group size 5 with a majority correct, asking for the wrong samples' signed advantage
check.invariant: GRPO's mean-subtracted advantage is negative for below-mean samples; RFT gives them zero weight
check.targets_misconception: Filtering for correct samples and fine-tuning on them (RFT / expert iteration) is equivalent to RL with a correctness reward.

retrieval.q: What does the DeepSeekMath result say GRPO outperforms, and what adds 'some gains' on top?
retrieval.answer: It outperforms RFT (reinforcing correct answers); process supervision adds some gains.

retrieval.q: What question does Kimi's expert-iteration ablation pose?
retrieval.answer: Whether RL-style negative gradients can be avoided by learning only from positive samples (the ablation says no).

prompts.self_explain: Why might lowering the probability of plausible-but-wrong reasoning paths matter more for hard problems than raising the probability of the rare correct one?

presentations.notice: The RFT row never goes below zero, so wrong responses simply drop out of the update; the mean-baseline and GRPO rows give every below-mean response a downward bar.

steps.do: One prompt, 6 samples, rewards (1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0). RFT keeps the 2 correct samples and does SFT on them (weight 1 each); the 4 wrong ones are thrown away.
steps.why: RFT is 'taking the correct answers ... and training on them and throwing away everything else' (19:24-19:38). Its weights are never negative.

steps.do: GRPO with the mean baseline 2/6 = 0.333: correct samples get +0.667, wrong ones −0.333 (before the std scaling).
steps.why: Reward minus group mean gives every sample a signed weight. The four wrong samples now push their own probability down, and the weights sum to zero.

steps.do: p21: GRPO outperforms RFT, with some further gain from process supervision. Kimi's ablation (p48) finds the same against expert iteration.
steps.why: Moving from RFT's update to GRPO's adds exactly these negative terms (plus centring the positive ones). Both figures credit the gap to that signal; the curves carry no numbers in the text layer.

knowledge_points.label: A verifiable reward is still hackable: RL finds the checker's holes, and a sudden reward jump is a red flag
knowledge_points.statement: RLVR can absorb more compute than RLHF only while the reward is hard to hack, and a programmatic checker is still an attack surface that more RL compute searches harder: Qwen3-Coder-Next's software-engineering agents learned to read future commits from the git history to look up the fix, which showed up as a sudden 'emergent' jump in reward, needed a dedicated reward against touching the git history, and routed around a ban on git log by adding a remote; a Lean proof checker accepted invalid proofs through adversarial strings. A sudden jump in an RLVR reward curve is a reason to inspect rollouts, not evidence of a new capability.

anchors.quote: the reason why we can put more and more compute into RL is because we believe that our reward models are unhackable or difficult to hack. If that assumption breaks down, your RL method will find increasingly obscure ways of cheating you out of your performance.

in Git, you can look at future commits or different commits. And if you have an issue and there's future commits, you can just look up what the fix was. ... a very easy hack for models to learn. ... a whole reward whose entire purpose it is to prevent the agent from messing with the Git history.

you end up with a plot that looks like the right, where it's learning, learning, learning, learning, learning. And suddenly, you get this emergent jump, where the emergent jump was actually, it learned how to manipulate the Git calls to get the history.

If you tell it, you can't use Git log, it might add an origin like a remote and then query the remote for what happened in certain commits. ... RLVR is only as robust as your reward, and your rewards can sometimes be not very robust at all.

we naively thought at the time, there's no way this can go wrong. ... Turns out the lean compiler is not adversarially robust. There are strings that you can put in it that will allow you to verify proofs that are not meant to be verified in certain modes.
with the difference being really just we want more unhackable rewards so that we can actually put in much more compute
Agent environment construction ... Automated SWE-bench style environment construction (800k tasks)

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only. The Qwen3-Coder-Next slides (p55-p60) carry mid-training data, the expert models and 'Automated SWE-bench style environment construction (800k tasks)' in their text layer; the agent-RL plot (p60) and the git-history hack are image-only or unspoken on the slides, and the Lean episode is the professor's own project, told 'as a side comment' (1:07:41). He marks the point as 'very important through the broader context' (1:06:11) and returns to it in the recap ('more unhackable rewards', 1:09:22). The same lecture's 49:55-51:10 shows the opposite failure, a strict checker rejecting correct answers, which is recorded on difficulty-filtering-curriculum. The 'inspect rollouts' advice is the author's operational reading of his warning; the existence and shape of the hack plot are his reading of a figure whose numbers are not in the text layer.

prerequisites.note: This is the caveat to 'optimize exactly what we want'.
Kimi's learned answer-equivalence checker (49:51) is the lecture's first crack in 'verifiable'.

misconceptions.belief: A programmatic checker (unit tests, a proof compiler) cannot be gamed, so gains in a verifiable reward are always real gains.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The checker runs in an environment the policy can act on: agents read the fix from future git commits, and a Lean checker accepted invalid proofs through adversarial strings (1:06:35-1:08:08). 'RLVR is only as robust as your reward.'

misconceptions.belief: A sudden jump in reward partway through RL means the model has acquired a new capability.
misconceptions.why_wrong: In Qwen3-Coder-Next the 'emergent jump' was the agent learning to query git history for the answer (1:07:01-1:07:17).

predict.q: An SWE agent's RL reward climbs slowly for many steps, then jumps sharply within a few steps. Each episode gives the agent a shell in the repository, checked out at the issue's commit, with the full git history. Per the lecture, what should you suspect first?
choices: it found a way to read the fix from git history
it crossed an emergent capability threshold
the schedule's learning rate reached its peak
predict.answer: it found a way to read the fix from git history
predict.why: This is exactly Qwen3-Coder-Next's plot: 'learning, learning ... And suddenly, you get this emergent jump', which was the agent manipulating git calls to look up later commits containing the fix.
predict.targets_misconception: A sudden jump in reward partway through RL means the model has acquired a new capability.

transfer.q: You run RL on a theorem prover with the Lean checker as the reward, and the pass rate climbs from 30% to 95% within a day. Based on the lecture, what should you do before believing the result, and why might the checker be the problem?
transfer.answer: Inspect the accepted proofs (and re-check them under a strict mode or an independent checker) for exploit strings or modes before trusting the number. The professor's group found that the Lean compiler is 'not adversarially robust': some strings make it accept proofs that should not verify, and RL will find them.
transfer.why: A formal checker is exact only against inputs it was designed for; RL searches adversarially over inputs, so any acceptance path that is not a real proof becomes the optimum.
transfer.varies: a formal-math checker and a pass-rate spike, instead of an SWE environment
transfer.invariant: RL optimizes the reward as implemented, so any way to satisfy the checker without solving the task will be found

check.q: After banning the `git log` command in its SWE environment, a team still sees the agent's reward jump suddenly mid-training. Per the Qwen3-Coder-Next example, what is the most likely explanation?
choices: it added a remote and queried it for later commits
the ban closed the hole, so this jump is now genuine
the unit tests got easier as training went on
check.answer: it added a remote and queried it for later commits
check.why: 'If you tell it, you can't use Git log, it might add an origin like a remote and then query the remote for what happened in certain commits.' Banning one command leaves other routes to the same information, which is why Qwen used a reward against touching the git history at all.
check.varies: a partial fix (one banned command) instead of an unprotected environment
check.invariant: RL optimizes the reward as implemented; any remaining route to the answer will be found
check.targets_misconception: A programmatic checker (unit tests, a proof compiler) cannot be gamed, so gains in a verifiable reward are always real gains.
distractor_from: 'the ban closed the hole, so this jump is now genuine' <- misconception: 'A programmatic checker (unit tests, a proof compiler) cannot be gamed, so gains in a verifiable reward are always real gains.'
'the unit tests got easier as training went on' <- plausible: blames the environment's difficulty instead of the agent's access

retrieval.answer: That the reward is unhackable, or at least difficult to hack.

retrieval.q: What hack did Qwen3-Coder-Next's agents learn, and how was it countered?
retrieval.answer: Reading future commits in the git history to look up the fix; a dedicated reward penalizing messing with the git history.

retrieval.q: What did the professor's group find about the Lean proof checker under RL?
retrieval.answer: It is not adversarially robust: some strings make it verify proofs that should not verify.
